Whether Manasseh's youth explains the apostasy, and whether it excuses any of it, is the first question. Ellicott allows the explanation: this early accession to power may help to account for his deviation from his father's religious policy, though it is not necessary to assume with Thenius that the queen-mother swayed the government until he reached a riper age, since Manasseh may have been older than his years. Henry grants the same influence and then refuses it as any excuse, on a comparison that settles the matter: his coming to the crown so young may help to account for it, and yet will by no means excuse him, for his grandson Josiah came to it younger still and acted well. Henry specifies two effects of the youth: he was puffed up with his honour and thought himself wise because he was great, valuing himself on undoing what his father had done, it being too common for novices to be lifted up with pride; and he was easily wrought upon by seducers who lay in wait, the enemies of Hezekiah's reformation flattering him, gaining his ear and using his power at their pleasure. Ellicott makes the same suggestion in passing, that he did evil perhaps under the pernicious influence of his courtiers. Henry adds the grim arithmetic that this was the only very bad reign in Judah that was also a long one, fifty-five years, longer than any other king's.

Ellicott alone supplies the imperial setting, and it changes how the reign looks. Manasseh was a tributary first to Esar-haddon and then to Assurbanipal, on the authority of the Assyrian inscriptions, which make the conclusion imperative that he paid tribute to the great king of Assyria. He observes that Manasseh's name, like that of his successor Amon, suggests Egyptian influence, and that combinations with Egypt against Assyria were popular at that epoch, which places the religious revolution inside a foreign policy rather than beside it. On the star-worship he notes that the Babylonian astrology and its concomitant superstitions had been introduced under Ahaz, so that Manasseh was reviving rather than inventing; and he quotes a modern scholar to the effect that the idols and sun-pillars and sacred trees and other half-pagan symbols were of the very substance of Israel's worship in the popular sanctuaries, and that from Manasseh onwards the worship of Moloch and of the Queen of Heaven appear as prominent new features of Judah's idolatry.

On the Asherah the two who discuss it agree against the English and then go further. Clarke says everyone may see that the word must signify an idol and not a grove, and identifies it with the Babylonian and Roman goddess known under other names. Ellicott reads the same word in the same way and locates the thing precisely: the image was erected within the temple itself, probably in the holy place, an act which was the climax of Manasseh's impiety. He is similarly exact about the altars, that the general statement of building them in the house of the Lord means the two courts, and that the particular notice includes even the inner and more sacred court where the sacrifices were offered to Jehovah. Clarke itemises the divinations: observing times means divination by the clouds, by their course and kinds and contrary directions; enchantments means incantations, spells and charms; dealing with familiar spirits means a necromancer and raiser of spirits; and the wizards are the knowing ones. Ellicott adds that the appointment was formal, a necromancer installed as a court official. On why the comparison with the dispossessed nations is so damning Ellicott gives the reason the others leave implicit: the idolatry of Judah was worse than that of the Canaanites because they worshipped only their own national gods, whereas Judah forsook its own God and was ready to adopt almost any foreign worship it came into contact with.
10:
Which prophets spoke the sentence the text leaves open, and Ellicott works through it carefully. The general expression is used, he says, because the historian found no name in his source; Isaiah may still have been living and may have protested in the manner described, but more probably the protests were his disciples', since the style is not Isaiah's. He weighs Ewald's stronger proposal, that the originality of the language a few verses later makes this an extract from the lost work the chronicler cites for the words of the seers who spoke to Manasseh; but he judges it much more likely that the passage is a summary of many such prophetic addresses. Henry does not ask who spoke but why, setting out the prophetic office in three stages: the prophets were sent first to teach the knowledge of God, then, if that failed, to reprove men that they might repent, and if that failed too, to foretell the judgments of God, either that the terror might awaken those whom his love could not, or that the execution might demonstrate the divine mission of those who foretold it. The prophets, Henry concludes, were deputed judges to those who would not receive them as teachers.

The figures of the sentence are read two different ways. On the line and plummet Clarke takes both measures dynastically: Jerusalem will be treated as Samaria was, pillaged and its people led into captivity; and since the house of Ahab was destroyed with not a man of his race left to sit on the throne of Israel, so the royal family of Judah shall be destroyed with none of their race to sit on the throne, nor shall Judah have a throne to sit on. Jerusalem has the same weight as well as the same measure as Samaria, having copied the abominations that brought that kingdom down. Ellicott reads the same figure architecturally, the measuring line and plummet suggesting Jerusalem levelled and laid even with the ground, the sense being that God will deal with the city by the same rigorous rule of judgment already used on Samaria. On the wiped dish Ellicott takes the wiping for the destruction of the people and the turning upside down for the overthrow of the city, allowing with Thenius that the two together may represent the single notion of making an end. Clarke finds an entirely different image by way of the Latin, which has God blotting out Jerusalem as tablets are blotted out, a metaphor from writing with a stile on boards spread with wax, one end sharp for tracing and the other blunt for rubbing out.

On the blood and its aftermath they supplement each other. Henry reads the indictment as a double count: Manasseh had done wickedly though he knew better, had justified the Amorites whose copy he wrote after by outdoing them in impieties, and had debauched the people of God whom he taught and forced to sin; and besides all that he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, multiplying his murders in every corner and filling the measure of its blood-guiltiness to the brim. Ellicott identifies the blood as the prophets' and their followers', and quotes an account of why the reaction came: the worship the prophets condemned and Hezekiah had proscribed was too deeply interwoven with life to be uprooted by royal decree, and the old prejudice of the country folk against the capital must have co-operated with superstition to produce a strong revulsion, so that a bloody struggle ensued between the conservative party and the followers of the prophets, the new king being on the side of the reaction. Ellicott records a reversal of scholarly opinion: the story of Manasseh's captivity and repentance, which the chronicler alone tells, is now allowed by the best critics to be genuine history, though it was once the fashion to call it an edifying fiction.
19:
Amon's two years draw a pattern from Clarke and a moral from Henry. Clarke reports that the rabbinical remark is not wholly without foundation, that the sons of idolatrous kings who succeeded their fathers seldom reigned more than two years, and gives four instances, Nadab son of Jeroboam, Elah son of Baasha, Ahaziah son of Ahab, and Amon himself. Henry asks why the successor was a son born when Manasseh was forty-five, and offers two possibilities: that Manasseh in his blind and brutish zeal for his idols had sacrificed his other sons, or that having been dedicated to those idols they were refused by the people. On the reign Henry reads the three charges as a single renunciation: Amon forsook the God of his fathers, disobeyed the commands given them and disclaimed their covenant, treading in the steps of his father's idolatry and reviving what his father in the latter end of his days had put down. From that Henry draws the warning that those who set bad examples, though they may repent themselves, cannot be sure that those whom they have drawn into sin will repent. Clarke makes the point more flatly, that we hear enough of this man when we hear he was as bad as his father was at first but did not copy his father's repentance. Ellicott adds a detail tying the reign to its predecessor: the name Amon is perhaps that of the Egyptian sun-god, which suits an idolatrous father.

The murder is read as retribution by one and left open by the others. Henry makes the symmetry explicit: his servants who should have guarded him murdered him, and his own house, which should have been his castle of defence, became the place of his execution; he had profaned God's house with his idols, and now God suffered his own house to be polluted with his blood, so that however unrighteous the doers were, God was righteous who suffered it. Clarke will not guess at the motive, saying we cannot tell what reason they had for slaying their king, but infers from the sequel that it was not a popular act, since the people of the land rose up and slew the regicides. Ellicott takes the servants, on the common use of the phrase, for courtiers or palace officials, and says plainly that nothing further is known of the circumstances. Henry notes that the people by their representatives did justice on the traitors and put them to death, since though Amon was a bad king he was their king.

Clarke closes the chapter with a sustained argument that the word our version renders grove means an idol, and it is the best philology here. Asherah, he holds, is undoubtedly the name of an idol, probably one carved out of wood. He assembles the authorities: Jarchi says it means a tree worshipped by the Gentiles, as the oak was worshipped by the ancient Druids in Britain; Castel's lexicon defines it as a wooden image dedicated to Astarte or Venus; Theodoret is cited as observing that the Greek word means Astarte and Venus and is called Ashtaroth by other interpreters; and the Targum of Ben Uzziel, where the command is to cut down their groves, translates instead that the oaks of their adoration shall be cut down. Then comes the argument that settles it for Clarke, taken from the next chapter rather than this one. Josiah is there said to have brought out the grove from the house of the Lord, which Clarke calls a very absurd translation, asking what grove there could have been in the temple, since none was planted there and there was no room for any; the plain meaning is that he brought out the goddess and burnt it. Ellicott had reached the same conclusion without the apparatus, placing the image in the holy place itself as the climax of Manasseh's impiety.
